text.p: THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A recent survey has found wage increases secured in enterprise bargaining agreements sat at six percent a year during the June quarter. This figure remains well above the "comfort zone" level needed for an interest rate cut by the Reserve Bank. Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith sized the opportunity to demand unions slow down any wage outcomes not linked to productivity gains. Page 1.

The Federal Opposition has demanded a full inquiry into the awarding of a A$1 million government advertising contract to an ad agency with strong Liberal Party connections. In a letter signed by Prime Minister Howard's political adviser, Grahame Morris, it has been revealed that Morris intervened in the advertising agency selection process. Page 3.

Qantas Airways has joined the growing chorus of tourism operators appealing for urgent action to revitalise tourism from Japan and to stop the general decline of Japanese tourists. Senior tourism authorities have cited steep air tickets, visa problems anda shortage of hotel infrastructure for the decline in Japanese travel. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Prime Minister John Howard is under further pressure for comprehensive tax reform following the National Party's push for a system overhaul. Howard and Deputy Prime Minister, National Party Leader Tim Fischer, were forced again to distance themselves from a goods and services tax after Senate Nationals' Leader Ron Boswell said the Nationals' wanted the consumption tax as part of the Coalition's second term agenda. Page 1.

Figures to be issued this week by AGB McNair NetWatch indicate Australia's Internet economy is facing a demographic overhaul as the network welcomes a new breed of Web surfer - older, richer and more likely to access the Internet more regularly. The figues point to the over-40 age group as the new force in Internet shopping and also show there are 60 percent more Internet users now than there were in March. Page 1.

Following the National Party Federal conference in Canberra, Federal Deputy Leader John Anderson has made a strong call for the party to improve its relations with our indigenous population and to examine ways in which it can more actively contribute to achieving the reconciliation process. Page 3.

Prime Minister John Howard and Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer have both declared the deportation of 10 Australians from Malaysia to be "unfortunate", but have defended Malaysia's right to deport the 36 foreigners arrested after storming an international conference on East Timor. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Drastic changes are being proposed for parliamentary procedure by the New South Wales Attorney-General's office, after the suicide last week of former Supreme Court judge David Yeldham. The changes would give politicians power to suppress the names of people cited under parliamentary privilege. Page 1.

The government has avoided any trouble with the Malaysian Government by accusing 10 Australians, arrested and deported from Malaysia by police after a banned conference in Kuala Lumpur on East Timor, of provoking a breach of immigration laws. Page 1.

South Australian Premier Dean Brown and his rival, Industry and Infrastructure Minister John Olsen, have refused to accept a factional peace proposal, effectively setting the scene for a leadership showdown. The peace proposal was doomed to fail as Olsen has said he would not serve as a replacement for Deputy Premier Baker and Brown has said he would not have him anyway. Page 1.

Criticism of SBS television on the Nine Network's Sunday programme has resulted in the SBS board referring allegations of financial mismanagement to its auditors and establishing a sub-committee to investigates the service's response to its chrter. However, SBS managing director Malcolm Long dismissed claims the response gives the Sunday report any foundation, saying the report was unethical and malicious. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The New South Wales Legal Aid Commission is to make further funding cuts, including withdrawing funding for inquests and for people taking anti-discrimination actions, refusing aid to tenants and residents of retirement villages who come before the Residential Tenancies Tribunal, withdrawing aid for appeals arising from criminal cases in local courts, and forcing people taking unfair dismissal actions to pay their own legal fees. The commission itself admits the cuts will have "horrific consequences" for needy people caught in civil or criminal proceedings. Page 1.

A Surfrider Foundation survey of 1,612 beaches around the country, titled Human Impact on Australian Beaches, has found Australia's beaches are under threat from developers, stormwater pollution, litter, and billions of litres of sewerage. The survey found public sewerage outfalls are discharging effluent near beaches at a rate of three billion litres a day. Page 1.

Prime Minister John Howard says detention of 10 Australians in Malaysia, who attended a Kuala Lumpur conference on East Timor that was banned by the Malaysia Government, was unfortunate. However, the government is refusing to protest the incident, which pro-East Timorese groups criticised. Page 1.

The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions has already processed information from four segments of the New South Wales Police Royal Commission hearings which are expected to see dozens of corrupt New South Wales Police criminally charged later this month. The Royal Commission has obtained evidence that will result in the biggest shake-out in the history of the state's police service. Page 3.
THE AGE

Singapore-based ABC journalist Catherine McGrath could face national security charges in Malaysia after a violent protest in Kuala Lumpur at a government-banned conference marking the anniversary of the Dili massacre. Along with McGrath, seven Australian, including a Melbourne bishop, are being expelled from Malaysia. Page A1.

As the Victorian government faces one of its most significant political uncertainties - the closure or merger of 113 Victorian schools - government strategists are working on reviving a plan to minimise the political damage from the moves. The strategy will give schools less than two months to decide on whether to merge or miss out on extra funding. Page A1.

According to an international study, the Australian leg of which was conducted by the Australian Consumers' Association, Australian children are exposed to more junk food advertisements on tv than children anywhere else in the world - 12 during an average hour of Australian children's television. Page A3.

Controversial British historian David Irving, whose application for an Australian visa was rejected last week, has threatened to sue Prime Minister John Howard for describing him as a "crackpot historian" and exaggerating his criminal record. If Irving does not receive an apology from Howard over the remarks, he has instructed his Australian solicitor to start defamation proceedings. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
